analysis.title: Peak AI Impulse: Goldman Says Wealth Effect Has Topped As Oil, Yields And Layoffs Gang Up On 2027, Reversing AI Boost
key_insights: Goldman chief economist Jan Hatzius estimates the AI-driven stock rally boosted US real consumer spending growth by about 0.4pp (0.25% of GDP) over the past year via the wealth effect. He expects that boost to decline over the next year.
In Goldman's downside case (AI stocks down 40%, other stocks down 15%), the wealth effect flips from a 0.5pp boost to roughly a 0.5pp drag on annualized consumption growth by Q3 2027.

Goldman says global growth in 2026 has been in line with potential. Fiscal easing and the AI boom offset the drag from the Iran war and higher US tariffs. Goldman sees world GDP growth at 2.7% in 2026 (consensus 2.6%) and 2.7% in 2027, with US growth slowing to 2.1% in 2027 from 2.3%.
Hatzius says the balance of risks for 2027 is on the downside. The 2027 forecast assumes lower energy prices offset fading fiscal and AI tailwinds.

Energy prices have climbed again on fears of renewed Middle East escalation. Gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and European/Asian natural gas are near or above their March/April highs. Brent closed just under $117 on Friday.

Goldman's commodity scenarios: in the base case, with 2027 Gulf supply 0.3mb/d below February levels, Brent falls toward $75 by late 2027. In the upside case, with Gulf supply 5mb/d short, Brent peaks above $140 next spring.

Morgan Stanley's Martijn Rats says refinery runs in Russia and the Middle East are about 3 million b/d below last year. Scheduled maintenance rises by 3.4 million b/d between 4Q26 and 2Q27, about 2.5x the norm, so product markets may tighten next.

Developed-market yields are up an average of about 100bp since early 2026. Goldman estimates a sustained rise subtracts a cumulative 0.6% from GDP through housing, consumer durables and business investment. Only part of this is in the forecasts because Goldman expects fewer central bank hikes than priced.

Goldman cites deficits, AI-linked borrowing and central bank hikes as drivers of higher long-term yields. The biggest hits come via housing in the US, Spain and the Netherlands, and via consumer credit in Sweden, Australia and Canada.

French bond turbulence has tightened euro area financial conditions enough to cut growth by 1/4 to 1/2pp annualized in coming quarters. Goldman frames the ECB's December choice as an expected final hike to 2.75% versus restarting bond buying.

Hatzius says the AI growth impulse was set to peak in late 2026 or early 2027. The increase in AI investment as a share of GDP is expected to slow, and last year's boost from US depreciation allowances is fading, which weighs on capital spending growth.
On consensus estimates, the year-over-year increase in hyperscaler investment peaks at about 1.5% of US GDP in Q4 2026 and falls to roughly 0.6% by the end of 2027.
The article says Meta decided to tap shareholders for up to $95 billion after the debt window closed. It cites Goldman's Rich Privorotsky saying the cost of capital for AI has objectively repriced.

Goldman sees AI labor effects spreading beyond tech. Across US nonmanufacturing industries, AI adoption share correlates negatively with employment growth (t-stat -2.07) and positively with unemployment (t-stat 4.20), now including finance, insurance and professional services.
The article tallies roughly 14,000 disclosed October job cuts in just over three weeks, and says the Dutch government announced plans to cut 25,000 civil servant jobs in an AI-led efficiency drive.

Goldman's strongest global view is that central banks will deliver fewer hikes than priced. For the Fed: no move at the October 28 meeting, one more 25bp hike to 4-4.25% on December 9, a possible additional hike in March if energy pushes inflation up, and renewed cuts in late 2027/early 2028.

Market pricing has the funds rate rising to around 4.5% by mid-2027. Goldman's scenario odds are 50% baseline, 35% three-hike scenario with a higher terminal rate, and 15% recession with the funds rate heading toward 1%.
JPMorgan's Michael Feroli expects a Fed hold this week with two hawkish dissents. September PPI showed the largest monthly rise in final-demand goods prices since the series began in 2009.
Goldman expects the BoE to hike 25bp to 4% on November 5 and says market pricing of 4+ hikes looks excessive. It also expects hikes in Canada and New Zealand this week and Australia next week.

Goldman's asset-class views: rates rally might extend, wary of momentum factor exposure in equities, S&P 500 to resume climbing after the midterms, caution on IG tech bonds with scope for near-term HY reversal, yen as a hedge against AI jitters, and targeted exposure to oil products and European gas plus longer-term copper, gold and power.

Since the AI rout began on October 14, the correlation between Goldman's AI Leaders basket and USDJPY has moved from -0.34 to +0.46. The yen remains the most undervalued currency on Goldman's GSDEER list.

Morgan Stanley's political team says a Democratic sweep is the most bearish midterm outcome for AI sentiment, bringing more durable and sweeping data center restrictions. Prediction markets give Republicans a slim chance of holding Congress.
HSBC moved to overweight developed-market government bonds from maximum underweight. Average CCC yields topped 16% on Friday for the first time since 2020.

tension_points.bull_case: Goldman's base case has growth at trend, fewer hikes than priced, and the S&P 500 higher after the midterms as earnings keep growing solidly. The wealth effect fades gradually if stocks perform in line with strategists' expectations.
tension_points.bear_case: If AI-related stocks keep falling, the wealth effect turns into a roughly 0.5pp drag on annualized consumption growth by Q3 2027. Energy, yields and AI-driven layoffs are all moving the wrong way.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A further decline in AI stocks (Goldman's downside case is AI stocks down 40%, other stocks down 15%) or Brent staying near $117 rather than falling toward $75.

tension_points.bull_case: Goldman expects fewer hikes than priced, with one more Fed hike in December and cuts in late 2027/early 2028 as disinflation arrives.
tension_points.bear_case: Upside inflation risks, most obviously energy, could bring another hike in March. Goldman gives 35% odds to a three-hike scenario with a higher terminal rate.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Energy-driven upside inflation surprises that bring a March hike, or a September PPI-type surge in goods prices.
